DSpace's Simple Archive Format is a directory with one subdirectory per item; each holds a file of the item's descriptive metadata and the item's files. The DSpace 7 documentation has details.

A collapsible view of a SAF archive: a top-level directory with one subdirectory per item. Each item directory holds dublin_core.xml (dc schema metadata), metadata_<prefix>.xml for other registered schemas, a contents file listing the files one per line, an optional collections file of handles (the first is the owning collection), an optional relationships file for entities, and the files themselves, added as bitstreams.
Opens the page on the filter-media script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The filter-media script processes the files added to DSpace, for example extracting full text so files can be searched, and creating thumbnails. The Media Filter documentation has more.
Only repository administrators may run the filter-media script.
The filter-media script is used to extract full text from documents and create thumbnails.

By default filter-media processes every bitstream and runs every Media Filter plugin listed in filter.plugins in dspace.cfg, extracting full text and creating thumbnails; parameters narrow which bitstreams and plugins are used.

filter-media parameters: -v verbose (prints the extracted text), -q quiet (errors only), -f force reprocessing of all bitstreams, -i only the given identifier, -m at most N items, -p only the named plugins (comma-separated), -s skip the given identifiers (comma-separated), -h help.
Quick guide: filter-media extracts full text and creates thumbnails for all bitstreams with all plugins by default, and its parameters restrict it to chosen bitstreams or plugins to save time.
Opens the page on the harvest script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The harvest script sets a collection to harvest its items from an external OAI-PMH server, either metadata only or files as well where the source supports it. The OAI documentation has more.
Only repository administrators may run the harvest script.
The harvest script sets up a collection for harvesting, runs harvests, and manages harvested collections: it can reset their status, purge them, and reimport all of a collection's items.
The harvest script uses OAI-PMH: for a collection set up for harvesting it connects to the given server, fetches metadata for the configured set and format, and creates or updates items in DSpace.

Harvest parameters: -p purge the collection's items, -r run a harvest, -g ping and set up the OAI server, -s set up the collection, -S start the harvest loop, -R reset harvest status on all collections, -P purge all harvestable collections, -o reimport (-p then -r), -c the collection, -t harvest type (0 for none), -a the OAI-PMH server address, -i the OAI set id, -m the metadata format (resolved in dspace.cfg), -h help.
Quick guide: the harvest script manages OAI-PMH harvesting of external collections, from setup through running to managing harvested collections.
Opens the page on the import script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.

The import script imports items or collections from Simple Archive Format (SAF), described on the export page. Its parameters set the action, the zip file, the destination collection, whether to use the collection's workflow, and whether to validate only.
Only repository administrators may run the import script.
The import script loads items from a SAF zip file, with options to add, replace or delete items, map them with a mapfile, send them through a collection's workflow, and more.
The import script unpacks a SAF zip and handles each item as the parameters say: adding it to a collection, replacing items listed in a mapfile, or deleting them.

Import parameters: -a add, -r replace items in the mapfile, -d delete items in the mapfile, -z the SAF zip, -c destination collection(s) by handle or id, -m the mapfile linking SAF items to DSpace items, -w send through the collection's workflow, -n send workflow notification emails, -v validate only (test run), -x leave out bitstreams, -p apply a template, -R resume a failed add, -q quiet, -h help.
Quick guide: the import script loads items from a SAF zip, with options to add, replace or delete, use a mapfile, go through a collection's workflow, and more.
Opens the page on the index-discovery script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The index-discovery script works on the Discovery Solr search index, adding, removing, updating or rebuilding it according to its parameters. The Discovery documentation has more.
Only repository administrators may run the index-discovery script.
The index-discovery script keeps the Discovery Solr index up to date: adding, removing, updating and rebuilding it.
The index-discovery script finds in the database the items, collections and communities to add, update or remove, and applies those changes to the Solr index.

index-discovery parameters: -r remove an object by handle, -i add or update an object by handle or UUID, -c clean out documents no longer in the database, -d delete all records, -b rebuild the index from scratch, -s rebuild the spellchecker (combinable with -b and -f), -f force reindexing even of up-to-date handles, -h help.
Quick guide: index-discovery manages the Discovery Solr index, adding, updating or removing objects and cleaning, emptying or rebuilding the index, so users can find content.
Heading for the index of available scripts; no text beyond the heading.
Points to the Processes and Scripts endpoint documentation for how scripts and processes are run through the REST API.

Lists the scripts documented in the contract: curate, export, filter-media, harvest, import, index-discovery, metadata-deletion, metadata-export, metadata-export-search, metadata-import, orcid-bulk-push, process-cleaner, retry-tracker, solr-database-resync and subscription-send.
Opens the page on the metadata-deletion script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The metadata-deletion script removes every value of a given metadata field from every item.
Only repository administrators may run the metadata-deletion script.
The metadata-deletion script is used to remove one metadata field from all items.
The metadata-deletion script finds all items holding the field and deletes all its values; this can take time on a large repository. The deletion is permanent and cannot be undone.
metadata-deletion parameters: -m the metadata field name, -l list the fields that can be deleted.
Quick guide: metadata-deletion removes a field from all items; back up the repository first in case values need restoring.
Opens the page on the metadata-export-search script, with its contents: what it does, who can use it, when, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The metadata-export-search script exports, as CSV, the metadata of the results of a Discovery search. The Batch Metadata Editing documentation has more.
Only repository administrators may run the metadata-export-search script.
The metadata-export-search script is used for reports or exports based on search criteria, and its CSV can be the starting point for offline bulk edits through Batch Metadata Editing.
The script runs a search through the Discovery search API with the given query and parameters and exports the results' metadata as CSV.

Parameters of the metadata-export-search script: -q/--query for the discovery search string (not URL encoded), -s/--scope for the UUID of the site, community or collection that limits the search, -c/--configuration for the Discovery configuration to use, -f/--filter for an advanced filter written <filter-name>,<filter-operator>=<filter-value> (for example author,authority=<uuid> or title,contains=sample text), and -h/--help.

Closing quick guide for the metadata-export-search script. It exports, as CSV, the metadata of the records that match a discovery search, so a chosen subset of records can be moved into other systems or analysed with other tools.

Title and table of contents of the metadata-export script page, with a link back to the script index. The page has the usual sections: what it does, who can use it, when to use it, how it works, parameters, and a quick guide.
The metadata-export script exports, in CSV, the metadata of one item, collection or community. The block points to the DSpace 7 Batch Metadata Editing documentation for more.
Only repository administrators can run the metadata-export script.

The metadata-export script is used for batch editing: export the metadata of items, collections or communities, change it in a spreadsheet or text editor, then load it back with the metadata-import script.

How the metadata-export script works. It reads the metadata of the given item, collection or community from the database and writes it to a CSV file. By default only the fields users normally edit (such as title, author and date) are exported; -a/--all adds the fields that are not normally changed, such as provenance.

Parameters of the metadata-export script: -i/--id for the id or handle of the item, collection or community to export, -a/--all to include fields that are not normally changed (for example provenance), and -h/--help.
Closing quick guide for the metadata-export script: export metadata to a spreadsheet or editor, change many items, collections or communities at once, then re-import with the metadata-import script.
Title and table of contents of the metadata-import script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).
The metadata-import script imports metadata from a CSV file after batch editing. The block points to the DSpace 7 Batch Metadata Editing documentation.
Only repository administrators can run the metadata-import script.
The metadata-import script is for large-scale changes, so that the metadata of many items can be updated in bulk.
How the metadata-import script works: it reads a CSV file of metadata and updates the matching items in DSpace, typically after a batch edit of many items.

Parameters of the metadata-import script: -f <file> for the CSV source file, -s for silent operation with no confirmation of changes (use with caution), -w to send new items through the collection workflow, -n to send notification emails when new items go through a workflow, -v to validate the CSV without importing, -t to apply the collection template to new items if one exists, and -h/--help.
Closing quick guide for the metadata-import script. It imports metadata after a batch edit. Take care with silent mode, and validate the CSV before importing.
Title and table of contents of the ORCID-bulk-push script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).

The ORCID-bulk-push script synchronises, in bulk, every ORCID entity waiting in the ORCID queue. It is part of the DSpace ORCID integration, and the block points to the ORCID Integration documentation.
Only repository administrators can run the ORCID-bulk-push script.
The ORCID-bulk-push script is used to make sure every entity in the ORCID queue is synchronised, including ones whose earlier synchronisation failed.

How the ORCID-bulk-push script works. It finds every entity in the ORCID queue and tries to synchronise each with ORCID. A failed entity is retried up to a maximum number of attempts, 10 by default and configurable in the ORCID configuration file. The -f option forces synchronisation even when that maximum has been reached.
The ORCID-bulk-push script has one parameter: -f/--force, which forces synchronisation and ignores the maximum number of attempts.

Closing quick guide for the ORCID-bulk-push script. It synchronises every queued ORCID entity so DSpace stays up to date with ORCID, retries failures up to the maximum, and -f forces synchronisation of entities that have already failed too often.
Title and table of contents of the process-cleaner script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).
The process-cleaner script removes old DSpace processes that are in a given state: RUNNING, FAILED or COMPLETED.
Only repository administrators can run the process-cleaner script.
The process-cleaner script is used to clear out old processes that are no longer needed and that accumulate and take up server resources.

How the process-cleaner script works. It finds processes in the chosen states and deletes them from the database. By default it deletes COMPLETED processes; -r adds RUNNING ones and -f adds FAILED ones.

Parameters of the process-cleaner script: -h/--help, -r/--running to delete RUNNING processes, -f/--failed to delete FAILED processes, and -c/--completed to delete COMPLETED processes, which is the default when no status is given.
Closing quick guide for the process-cleaner script: removing old processes frees server resources. Give the states of the processes to remove.
Title and table of contents of the retry-tracker script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).

The retry-tracker script retries failed commits to the OpenURLTracker, which records requests DSpace makes to external systems (such as DOI lookup services) and stores metadata about them in the database. The script is also used when exchanging usage statistics with IRUS.
Only repository administrators can run the retry-tracker script.
The retry-tracker script is used when requests to external systems have failed because of network or service problems and need to be sent again.

How the retry-tracker script works. It finds the URLs marked as failed in the OpenURLTracker table and sends those requests again, which helps after temporary network or service failures. The -a option adds a test URL to the table so the script can be tried without waiting for a real failure.

Parameters of the retry-tracker script: -a <value> adds a "failed" row with a URL, for testing only; -r retries every URL in the table of failed requests, including one added with -a; -h/--help prints help.

Closing quick guide for the retry-tracker script: it resends failed requests to external systems so they are not lost to temporary network or service problems, and is worth adding to the workflow when such failures are frequent.
Title and table of contents of the solr-database-resync script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).
The solr-database-resync script updates the database status of items in Solr.
Only repository administrators can run the solr-database-resync script.

The solr-database-resync script is used when the database and the Solr index disagree, for example after the database was changed outside DSpace or indexing failed, so that item statuses in Solr no longer match and search results are wrong.

How the solr-database-resync script works. Each item's metadata is stored in the database and indexed in Solr, where a status field says whether the item is in archive, withdrawn or discoverable. The script reads all items and their status from the Solr index, checks each against the database, updates the database status where needed, and then reindexes each item so Solr holds the correct status.
The solr-database-resync script takes no parameters.

Closing quick guide for the solr-database-resync script. It brings the database and the Solr index back in line, but it can change the status of many items, so use it only when needed and back up the database first. It can help diagnose and fix wrong search results or item statuses.
Title and table of contents of the subscription-send script page, with a link back to the script index and the usual sections (what, who, when, how, parameters, quick guide).

The subscription-send script sends the email notifications for DSpace subscriptions, which users can take out on communities, collections or items. The block points to the Email Subscriptions documentation.
Only repository administrators can run the subscription-send script.
The subscription-send script sends periodic email updates at each user's chosen subscription frequency.

How the subscription-send script works. It runs periodically (for example daily) on the server, finds the users subscribed to communities, collections or items, and sends an email notification for each subscription. Its frequency parameter sets how often notifications go out; for example W sends them once a week.
The subscription-send script has one parameter: -f/--frequency <value>, the subscription frequency, which is D (day), W (week) or M (month).

Closing quick guide for the subscription-send script: it emails users about the items they subscribed to. It runs daily by default and the frequency can be changed; it can also help diagnose users not receiving their subscription emails.
Title of the Discovery Search Endpoints page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.

The /api/discover/search endpoint exposes the Discovery search screen's configuration so a client can build complex searches. It takes scope (the UUID of a site, community or collection; a scope-specific configuration in discovery.xml is used if one exists, else the default) and configuration (a named Discovery configuration, ignored when the scope already has one; the special workspace and workflow configurations always exist for MyDSpace). The response lists the advanced search filters (each with a type, whether it has facets, whether it is open by default, and its supported operators: equals, notequals, authority, notauthority, contains, notcontains) and the available sort options (score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned). It links to objects (the matching results) and facets (facet values and counts).

The /api/discover/search/objects endpoint returns the DSpace objects matching a search. Parameters: query (a Solr/Lucene query; special characters must be percent-encoded), dsoType (all, item, community or collection), scope (container UUID), configuration (ignored if the scope has its own), filters written f.<filter-name>=<value>,<operator> where name and operator must come from the parent search endpoint (an absent or invalid operator gives 422 Unprocessable Entity), and page, size and sort (a sort name from the parent endpoint or default, then a direction). The example response echoes the query, scope, applied filters and sort, and embeds a paginated list of search results, each with hit highlights and the indexable object, plus the facets for the query (author, subject and a dateIssued facet with min and max values and date-range buckets), each value linking to a refined search.

The /api/discover/search/facets endpoint returns the configured facets and their values for a search. It takes the same refinements as the objects search: query (a Lucene/Solr query; escape special characters to search them literally), a repeatable dsoType, scope, configuration, f.<filter-name>=<value>,<operator> filters (invalid operator gives 422), and page, size and sort. Some facets can be configured in discovery.xml to expose minimum and maximum values, as dateIssued does in the example. The example response echoes the query, filters and sort and embeds a paginated list of facets (author, subject, dateIssued), each with its values, counts and links to refined searches and to the next page.

The /api/discover/facets endpoint lists the facet fields that can be queried in the Discovery (Solr-based) facet system. It takes scope and configuration, with the same fallback rules as the search endpoint, and the facets returned depend on the Discovery configuration in discovery.xml. The example response is a paginated list of facets (author, subject, dateIssued with hasMinMaxValues, and has_content_in_original_bundle), each with a type, a limit and a self link.

The /api/discover/facets/<facet-name> endpoint lists the values of one facet. It can be refined by query, scope, f.<filter-name>=<value>,<operator> filters (an absent or invalid operator gives 422) and page, size and sort, where sort is count (descending number of matching records) or index (alphabetical). The example response for the author facet echoes the query and filters and returns paginated values, each with a label, count, authority key and a link to the search restricted to that value.
Heading for the special Discovery configurations, workspace and workflow, described in the next two blocks.

The workspace Discovery configuration returns every submission made by the current user, whatever its status: workspace items, workflow items and archived items. The example search result lists two workspace items and one workflow item (each with its sections, such as license, upload and traditionalpageone metadata, and links to its collection, item, submission definition and submitter), with facets namedresourcetype (Workspace, Workflow), itemtype and dateIssued.

The workflow Discovery configuration returns the workflow tasks relevant to the current user: pool tasks that can be claimed and tasks already claimed. The example search result lists two pool tasks in reviewstep with claimaction, each linking to its eperson, group and workflow item, with facets namedresourcetype (Waiting for Controller), itemtype, dateIssued and submitter.

Search methods on collection endpoints. A collection endpoint such as /api/core/{model} may expose search methods that return a subset of its resources, for example /api/core/communities/search/top for top-level communities or /api/submission/workspaceitems/search/findBySubmitter?uuid=<submitter-uuid>. All search methods of a resource are listed as a HAL document at /api/core/{model}/search, and each is exposed at /api/core/{model}/search/{method-name}. Discovery search is a separate topic.

The endpoints that have search methods: /api/core/communities, /api/core/metadatafields, /api/config/submissiondefinitions, /api/submission/workspaceitems, /api/workflow/claimedtasks, /api/workflow/polltasks and /api/workflow/workflowitems.
Title of the Signposting Endpoints page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.

The /signposting endpoints implement Signposting, which makes the scholarly web friendlier to machines by giving typed links, in HTTP Link headers and, for HTML, in link elements. DSpace supports the FAIR signposting profile at level 2.

Signposting main endpoint and the JSON linkset. /signposting/linksets is not implemented and returns 405, since there is no use case for listing all linksets. /signposting/linksets/<uuid>/json returns, in application/linkset+json, the typed links for an item and its files: item (bitstream downloads with their media types), type (schema.org AboutPage), linkset, describedby (DataCite XML), cite-as (the handle), author (an ORCID), license, and for each bitstream a collection link back to the item; a describes link ties the description back to the item. Return codes: 200 OK, 403 Forbidden without permission to read the item, 404 Not found if the item does not exist.

Two more signposting endpoints. /signposting/linksets/<uuid> returns the same typed links in application/linkset serialization (a list of <url>; rel=...; type=...; anchor=... entries covering item, describedby, cite-as, author (ORCID and ISNI), linkset, type, collection and describes). /signposting/links/<uuid> returns, as a JSON array of href, rel and type, the typed links for an item or bitstream to put in that page's response header or meta tags. Both return 200 OK, 403 Forbidden without permission to read the item, or 404 Not found.

The /signposting/describedby/<uuid> endpoint returns a description of the object in a commonly used format; the example is DataCite kernel-3 XML with title, DOI and URI alternate identifiers and Accepted and Available dates. Return codes: 200 OK, 403 Forbidden without permission to read the item, 404 Not found.
Title of the Displaying usage statistics page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.
GET /api/statistics/usagereports, the main usage-report endpoint, is not implemented and returns 405, since there is no use case for listing all reports.

GET /api/statistics/usagereports/<id> returns one usage report. The id joins the object's UUID and the report type, for example <uuid>_TopCountries. A report holds points whose type can be country, city, bitstream, item, collection, community or date, and the supported report types are TotalVisits, TotalVisitsPerMonth, TotalDownloads, TopCountries and TopCities. Responses: 200 OK; 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden when the statistics are not open to anonymous users and the caller is not authenticated or lacks permission; 404 Not Found.

GET /api/statistics/usagereports/search/object returns a paginated list of usage reports for one DSpace object, named by the uri parameter (the full REST URI of the resource), with the usual page and size parameters. The examples show reports for a site and for an item, such as TotalVisits with view counts. Responses: 200 OK; 400 Bad Request for a badly formed uri; 401 or 403 when the statistics are not open to anonymous users.
Title of the Collecting user interactions page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.
POST /api/statistics/viewevents records a page view. The parameters are described in the next blocks; everything else about the interaction is taken from the request itself.
Required parameters of a view event: targetId, the id of the object viewed, and targetType, its type.
Optional parameter of a view event: referrer, the referrer of the object viewed; if absent it is taken from the request.
Status codes of the view events endpoint: 201 Created on success, 400 Bad request if a parameter is missing or invalid, 422 Unprocessable Entity if the parameters do not point to a valid object.
Example body of an item page view event: a targetId UUID, targetType item, and a referrer URL.
POST /api/statistics/searchevents records a search. The parameters are described in the next blocks; everything else about the interaction is taken from the request itself.

Required parameters of a search event: query (the Discovery search string), page (an object giving the pagination state) and sort (an object giving the sort state), both as described in the pagination documentation.

Optional parameters of a search event: dsoType (all, item, community or collection), scope (the UUID of the container the search was limited to), configuration (the Discovery configuration used) and appliedFilters (the array of search filters applied, as in the search documentation).
Status codes of the search events endpoint: 201 Created on success, 400 Bad request if a required parameter is missing or a parameter is invalid.
Example body of a search event: a query, a scope UUID, the default configuration, applied filters, and the page and sort objects.

Download and workflow statistics need no client call. REST records file downloads itself, because the download always passes through REST even when the UI is not involved (for example a direct link from Google), and the internal workflow already records workflow action statistics.

Overview of submitting a new item through the REST API. Submission and workflow is one of the most used DSpace features and, being configurable, uses many endpoints. Every step needs authentication and a valid CSRF token: send the Authorization header and the CSRF token with every request.

Starting a submission means creating a WorkspaceItem, the in-progress submission object, with POST /api/submission/workspaceitems?owningCollection=<collection-uuid>, since every item belongs to a collection. This creates an empty WorkspaceItem by default; a multipart POST can instead start it from an uploaded file or from an external entry whose metadata is imported.

Modifying a submission. The response to the create call is the new WorkspaceItem; keep its id, which is needed to read or update it (GET /api/submission/workspaceitems/<id>). The item lists the sections to complete, which correspond to /api/config/submissionsections; each section's name is its id, and its sectionType says how to work with it. The section types are submission-form (metadata), upload (files), access (access rights and embargo), license (accepting the required licence) and cclicense (an optional Creative Commons licence), each documented separately.

Completing a submission means sending it into the approval workflow by POSTing the WorkspaceItem to the workflow items endpoint. Approval workflow is set per collection and is off by default. Without a workflow the item becomes available at once and keeps the UUID it had as a WorkspaceItem; with one, a WorkflowItem is returned and can be read at /api/workflow/workflowitems/<id>.
Title of the SubmissionAccessOptions Endpoints page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.
/api/config/submissionaccessoptions lists the SubmissionAccessConfig configurations, each of which gathers in one place the settings the submission access section needs.

/api/config/submissionaccessoptions/<config-name> returns one access configuration. canChangeDiscoverable says whether the submitter may choose if the item is findable through search and browse. Each entry in accessConditionOptions has a name, which the UI can show (translated through i18n) and the backend uses to build the resource policy; if hasStartDate is true a start date is required, no later than maxStartDate when that is set; if hasEndDate is true an end date is required, no later than maxEndDate when set, and after any start date. A null accessConditionOptions means the submitter cannot set a policy and the item gets only the policies inherited from its collection.

Introduction to the Submission CC Licenses endpoints. The structure follows the configuration options of DSpace 6 and earlier. The first implementation expects a single site-level configuration named default; having an endpoint for a collection of configurations leaves room for different setups for different kinds of submission, such as theses, technical reports or journal articles.

/api/config/submissioncclicenses lists the Creative Commons licences configured for the repository, corresponding to the Creative Commons REST API (version 1.5) filtered to those licences. The example returns a paginated list with entries such as publicdomain.

/api/config/submissioncclicenses/<license-name> returns one Creative Commons licence. A basic licence, such as publicdomain (CC0), has no fields; others, such as standard, have fields, which are the questions to answer when assigning the licence, each with a label, description and allowed values.

/api/config/submissioncclicenseurls/search/rightsByQuestions returns the final Creative Commons licence URI once the licence's questions are answered. First read the licence with /api/config/submissioncclicenses/<license-name>. Parameters: license (a licence id from the list, such as standard or publicdomain) and answer_<field-id>=<value-id> for each answer (for example answer_commercial=y&answer_derivatives=sa); answers are needed only if the licence asks for them. A valid combination returns the licence URL. Response codes: 200 OK, 400 Bad Request for invalid or missing answers, 401 Unauthorized if not logged in, 404 Not found for an unknown licence.

Introduction to the Submission-Definitions endpoints. A submission definition is set globally or per collection and describes a whole submission process as a series of sections (called steps before DSpace 7).
/api/config/submissiondefinitions lists the configured submission definitions. The example is still to be provided.

/api/config/submissiondefinitions/<definition-name> returns one submission definition, with its name (for example traditional), whether it is the default, and its type. It links to collections, the collections that explicitly use it, and sections, the submission sections it includes.
Heading for the search methods of the submission definitions endpoint.

Search method findByCollection, /api/config/submissiondefinitions/search/findByCollection?uuid=<collection-uuid>, returns the submission definition that applies to a collection, falling back to the default configuration.
Heading for the linked entities of a submission definition.

/api/config/submissiondefinitions/<definition-name>/collections lists the collections that explicitly use the submission definition. A collection that names no definition gets the default mapping but is not listed here.
/api/config/submissiondefinitions/<definition-name>/sections lists the submission sections used in the definition, as described on the submission sections page.

Introduction to the Submission-Forms endpoints. A submission form is one configurable data entry form, made of one or more fields and tied to a submission section. DSpace 6 and earlier called it an input-form, configured in input-forms.xml.

/api/config/submissionforms lists the configured submission forms. Since DSpace 7 the old input-forms.xml is split by page: each submission form is one page of inputs, and pages are combined by the submission definition (item-submission.xml). The example is still to be provided.

/api/config/submissionforms/<form-name> returns one submission form, for example traditionalpageone, as an ordered array of rows of fields. Each field has: input (the widget type, such as onebox, dropdown, date, lookup or lookup-name, and an optional validation regex; dropdown and lookup need a controlled vocabulary, and onebox gives auto-suggest, or the selection tree for a hierarchical vocabulary); scope (null, workflow or submission) with visibility (editable when null, readonly, or hidden); label; mandatory and mandatoryMessage; repeatable; hints; style (CSS classes); selectableMetadata (one or more metadata keys, each with an optional controlled vocabulary and label, the list form coming from qualdrop_value); selectableRelationship (relationship type, filter, Discovery search configuration, external sources and whether name variants are allowed); languageCodes (display and code pairs); and typeBind (the publication types the field applies to; empty means all). The selectable metadata and relationship attributes are exposed as strings for simplicity rather than as HAL links.

Table of the submission section types available out of the box in DSpace 7, with the endpoint that holds each one's extra configuration and the page documenting its data in a workspace item: collection (no configuration; data is the collection UUID), submission-form (/config/submissionforms), upload (/config/submissionuploads), license (taken from the collection's license link), cclicense (/config/submissioncclicenses), access (/config/submissionaccessoptions), sherpaPolicies (none) and identifiers (none).

Introduction to the Submission-Sections endpoints. A submission section is one section of the submission process. A submission-form section has a configurable input form; other section types, such as file upload, embargo and access rights or Creative Commons licensing, are not all configurable. The available section types are listed on their own page.
/api/config/submissionsections lists the configured submission sections. The example is still to be provided.

/api/config/submissionsections/<section-name> returns one submission section, with an id, a header (the label or i18n key shown to the user), mandatory (whether every submission must use the section; otherwise the user may enable or disable it), scope (null, or workflow or submission to limit the section to that phase), sectionType (the kind of section the UI must use; see the section types page) and a config link.
Heading for the linked entities of a submission section.

The config link of a submission section points to its detailed configuration, which depends on the section type: for example the fields of a form section, or the upload and access condition options of an upload section.

Introduction to the SubmissionUploads endpoints. The structure follows the configuration options of DSpace 6 and earlier. The first implementation expects a single site-level configuration named default; an endpoint for a collection of configurations leaves room for different setups for different kinds of submission, such as theses, technical reports or journal articles.

/api/config/submissionuploads lists the SubmissionUploadConfig configurations, each of which gathers what the upload section needs, such as the maximum file size and the access condition options. The example is still to be provided.

/api/config/submissionuploads/<upload-name> returns one upload configuration; the name starts out hard-coded to default. It holds whether an upload is required, the maximum file size (536870912 bytes in the example) and accessConditionOptions. Each option's name is shown by the UI (translated through i18n) and used by the backend to build the resource policy on the uploaded file; hasStartDate and hasEndDate require a start or end date, bounded by maxStartDate and maxEndDate when set, and an end date must follow the start date. A null accessConditionOptions means the submitter cannot set a policy and the file inherits the collection's policies. A metadata link points to the submission form for the file metadata.
Heading for the linked entities of an upload configuration.
The metadata link of an upload configuration, /api/config/submissionupload/<upload-name>/metadata, returns the submission form used for the files' metadata.
Introduction to the Subscriptions endpoints, which hold all the subscriptions requested.

GET /api/core/subscriptions returns a paginated list of all subscriptions, ordered by the UUID of the subscribed object. Each subscription has an id, a subscription type, a parameter list (such as frequency) and links to its eperson and resource. Return codes: 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized if not authenticated, 403 Forbidden for anyone but administrators.

GET /api/core/subscription/<id> returns one subscription. subscriptionType is currently only content, with room for others such as statistics. The parameter list currently supports only frequency, whose values are D (day), W (week) and M (month). Status codes: 200 OK for an administrator or the subscription's owner; 401 or 403 otherwise; 404 if it does not exist.
Heading for the search methods of the subscriptions endpoint.

Search method findByEPerson, GET /api/core/subscription/search/findByEPerson?uuid=<eperson-uuid>, returns a paginated list of the subscriptions of one eperson; uuid is mandatory. Status codes: 200 OK; 400 Bad Request for a missing or invalid uuid; 422 if the uuid is not an eperson; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for anyone but a system administrator or that eperson.

Search method findByEPersonAndDso, GET /api/core/subscriptions/search/findByEPersonAndDso?resource=<id>&eperson_id=<id>, returns the subscriptions a person holds on one community, collection or item; both parameters are mandatory, and page and size are supported. Status codes: 200 OK; 400 for missing or invalid parameters; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for anyone but a system administrator or that eperson.

Creating a subscription: POST /api/core/subscriptions?eperson_id=<uuid>&resource=<uuid>, both mandatory, with a body whose subscriptionType must be content and whose single parameter must be frequency with value D (day), W (week) or M (month). Return codes: 200 OK with the new subscription; 400 if a parameter is missing or not a UUID; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for anyone but a system administrator or the owner; 422 for an invalid type, parameter name or value.

Updating a subscription: PUT /api/core/subscription/<id> with a JSON body of the same form as for creation (type content, parameter frequency with value D, W or M). Return codes: 200 OK with the subscription; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for anyone but a system administrator or the owner; 422 for an invalid type, parameter name or value.

Deleting a subscription: DELETE /api/core/subscriptions/<id>. Return codes: 204 No content on success; 401 if not authenticated; 403 unless the caller owns the subscription or is an administrator; 404 if it does not exist or was already deleted.
Heading for the linked entities of a subscription.
GET /api/core/subscriptions/<id>/eperson returns the eperson the subscription belongs to. Return codes: 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 if the subscription does not exist.

GET /api/core/subscriptions/<id>/resource returns the community, collection or item the subscription is on. Return codes: 200 OK, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 if the subscription does not exist.
Introduction to the Supervision Orders endpoints, used to create, manage and find supervision orders.
/api/core/supervisionorders returns a paginated list of every supervision order in the system.

/api/core/supervisionorders/<id> returns one supervision order: its id, and links to the item it is defined on and the group allowed to supervise that item. Status codes: 200 OK; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for non-administrators; 404 if it does not exist.
Heading for the search methods of the supervision orders endpoint.

Search method byItem, /api/core/supervisionorders/search/byItem?uuid=<item-uuid>, returns the supervision orders on one item; uuid is mandatory. Return codes: 200 OK, including when the item has none; 400 for a missing or malformed uuid; 404 if no item matches.

Creating a supervision order: POST /api/core/supervisionorders?uuid=<item>&group=<group>&type=<type>, all mandatory. The type sets what the group's members are granted: NONE (nothing), EDITOR (read and write on the item and its bitstreams) or OBSERVER (read on the item and its bitstreams). A sample curl call is given. Return codes: 201 Created; 401 if not authenticated; 400 for a missing or malformed uuid or group, or one of the wrong object type; 403 for non-administrators; 422 if the item or group does not exist, the group already has an order on the item, or the item is not an in-progress submission (orders can only be made during submission or workflow).

Deleting a supervision order: DELETE /api/core/supervisionorders/<id>, with a sample curl call. Return codes: 204 No content; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for non-administrators; 404 if it does not exist.

Introduction to the system-wide alerts endpoints, which expose alerts shown as banners in the frontend. Only administrators create and edit alerts; everyone can view them, but regular users see only active ones. DSpace currently supports a single alert, though the endpoints allow for several, and the per-alert session restriction is a placeholder because session control is not implemented yet.
GET /api/system/systemwidealerts/search/active returns all active alerts, which the UI uses to decide what to show. It is the only alert endpoint non-administrators need. Status: 200 OK.

GET /api/system/systemwidealerts/<alert-id> returns one alert by its integer id, with its message, allowSessions, countdownTo date and active flag. An inactive alert is visible only to administrators; to anyone else it looks as if it does not exist. Status codes: 200 OK, or 404 for an inactive alert requested by a non-administrator.
GET /api/system/systemwidealerts returns every system-wide alert, inactive ones included. Status codes: 200 OK, 401 if not logged in, 403 for non-administrators.

Creating an alert: POST /api/system/systemwidealerts, for administrators, with a body giving message, allowSessions, countdownTo (a UTC datetime string) and active. allowSessions is all (allow all sessions), current (only current sessions; administrators can still log in) or admin (only administrators; other users are logged out). Status codes: 201 Created; 400 if an alert already exists; 401 if not logged in; 403 for non-administrators; 422 if the body cannot be parsed.

Modifying an alert: PUT /api/system/systemwidealerts/<alert-id>, for administrators, with the same body fields and allowSessions values as creation, and countdownTo as a UTC datetime string. Status codes: 200 OK; 401 if not logged in; 403 for non-administrators; 404 if no such alert; 422 if the body cannot be parsed.

Introduction to the versioning endpoints, which give access to a single version of an item. If versioning.item.history.view.admin is true, only community, collection or repository administrators can read versions; otherwise they are public. A version's access is independent of its item's, so a version of an item the user cannot see may still be read, which the text says is safe because a version exposes nothing sensitive.
/api/versioning/versions, the main versions endpoint, is not supported and returns 405 Method Not Allowed: versions are reached from an item or a version history, or directly by id.

Creating a version: POST /api/versioning/versions with an optional summary parameter and a text/uri-list body holding the URI of the item to version, which may have no history yet or belong to one (an older version can be used, to help restore it). Item administrators, and the original submitter if versioning.submitterCanCreateNewVersion allows, may do this. The new version is returned. Status codes: 201 Created; 401 if not authenticated; 403 without permission, or for an entity item while versioning.block.entity is true or unset; 400 if the URI is not an item; 422 if a new version is already in progress in the same history.

GET /api/versioning/versions/<versionId> returns one version: id, version number, created date, summary and, for an administrator of the item or when versioning.item.history.include.submitter is true, submitterName, with links to the version history and the item. What is returned depends on permissions and configuration. Status codes: 200 OK; 401 or 403 when versioning is not public and the caller is unauthenticated or lacks permission; 404 if the version does not exist.
To get the version of an item, follow the version link on the item endpoint.
A version is removed by deleting the item linked to it.

Updating a version. Only the summary can be changed, by item administrators; every other property is read-only and changing it gives 422. Item metadata is changed through the items, workspace items or workflow items endpoints, depending on the item's status. The summary is changed by a PATCH on /summary following the general patch rules: remove clears it, replace or add replaces it, add sets it when empty; a curl example is given, and an Authorization header is needed. Return codes: 200 OK, 401, 403, 404 if the version does not exist, and other codes per the patch rules.
Heading for the linked entities of a version.
The versionhistory link of a version returns its version history, described on the Version history page.
The item link of a version returns the item that matches this version.

Introduction to the version history endpoints. A version history groups all related versions. If versioning.item.history.view.admin is true, only community, collection or repository administrators can read histories; otherwise they are public. Access to a history is independent of its items, so a history of items the user cannot see may still be read, which the text says is safe because neither histories nor versions expose sensitive information.
/api/versioning/versionhistories, the main version histories endpoint, is not supported and returns 405 Method Not Allowed: histories are reached from a version item or directly by id.

GET /api/versioning/versionhistories/<versionHistoryId> returns one version history, with its id and draftVersion, which is true when the latest version's item is still in progress (workspace or workflow) and is shown only to users allowed to create a new version in that history. Status codes: 200 OK; 401 or 403 when versioning is not public and the caller is unauthenticated or lacks permission; 404 if a permitted user asks for a history that does not exist.
Heading for the linked entities of a version history.

GET /api/versioning/versionhistories/<versionHistoryId>/versions returns a paginated list of the history's versions, newest version number first, with attributes secured as for a single version. Only versions of archived or withdrawn items are listed, so the latest version is left out until it is archived. Return codes: 200 OK; 401 or 403 when versioning is not public.

GET /api/versioning/versionhistories/<versionHistoryId>/draftVersion gives access to the workspace or workflow item of the latest version when it is not yet archived. It follows the security of those endpoints, so a user allowed to create versions may still not see it; the draftVersion flag lets the UI turn off the create-new-version button in that case, and anonymous users cannot learn that a new version is under review.
Introduction to the Controlled Vocabularies endpoints. All of them are open to anonymous users.

/api/submission/vocabularies lists the configured controlled vocabularies, as a paginated list in which each vocabulary (for example srsc) has its scrollable, hierarchical and preloadLevel settings and an entries link.

/api/submission/vocabularies/<vocabulary-name> returns one controlled vocabulary. id and name are the same alphanumeric value; scrollable means all entries can be browsed without a filter; hierarchical means entries form a tree; preloadLevel, for hierarchical vocabularies, is the depth to which the tree should be preloaded (0 for top nodes only, 1 to include their children, and so on). An entries link gives the vocabulary's entries.
Heading for the linked entities of a controlled vocabulary.

/api/submission/vocabularies/<vocabulary-name>/entries returns vocabulary entries for a user's input or as a scrollable list. Parameters: page and size, filter (terms, keywords or a prefix), exact (true to match the filter exactly; default false) and entryID (the entries for one vocabulary entry id). Exactly one of filter and entryID must be given, except for scrollable vocabularies, which can be browsed freely. Return codes: 200 OK; 400 if both filter and entryID are given, or exact is invalid or given without filter; 401 if not authenticated; 422 if neither is given and the vocabulary is not scrollable. Samples show the common_types value-pairs vocabulary (paged, and filtered by Book), the hierarchical srsc vocabulary filtered by Research, and an authority vocabulary (SolrAuthorAuthority) whose entries carry an authority key.
Heading for the search methods of the controlled vocabularies endpoint.

Search method byMetadataAndCollection, /api/submission/vocabularies/search/byMetadataAndCollection?metadata=<schema.element[.qualifier]>&collection=<collection-uuid>, returns the controlled vocabulary configured for that metadata field and collection, in the same form as a single vocabulary, or an empty body if there is none. Return codes: 200 OK with a vocabulary; 204 No content if none is configured; 400 for missing or malformed parameters; 401 if not authenticated; 422 if the metadata field or collection does not exist.
Introduction to the Vocabulary Entries endpoints. All of them are open to anonymous users.
/api/submission/vocabularyEntryDetails, the main vocabulary entries endpoint, is not allowed: entries can only be fetched in subsets through the filters described next.

/api/submission/vocabularyEntryDetails/<vocabulary-name>:<entry-id> returns one vocabulary entry: its unique id, value (the preferred value to store), display (the preferred value to show), selectable (a hierarchical vocabulary may allow only leaves to be chosen) and otherInformation (a map of extra strings that give the UI more context). It links to its vocabulary and, in hierarchical vocabularies, to its parent and children. Return codes: 200 OK; 404 if the entry is missing or the id malformed; 401 if not authenticated.
Heading for the search methods of the vocabulary entries endpoint.

Search method top, /api/submission/vocabularyEntryDetails/search/top?vocabulary=<vocabulary-id>, returns a paginated list of the top entries of a hierarchical vocabulary; the example lists top entries of srsc such as HUMANITIES and RELIGION. Return codes: 200 OK; 400 for a missing or invalid vocabulary; 401 if not authenticated; 422 if the vocabulary exists but is not hierarchical.
Introduction to the Workflow Actions endpoints. A workflow action is one action in the review process, such as accept or reject. The endpoints need authentication but no specific permission.
/api/config/workflowactions, the main workflow actions endpoint, is not implemented and returns 405.

/api/config/workflowactions/<action-name> returns one workflow action. Its options are the actions the user may take in the step: edit_metadata means the user can PATCH the workflow item's submission sections, and the others are commands POSTed to the claimed task. advanced is false by default and true when advancedOptions is not empty, meaning the action needs more than plain buttons; advancedInfo carries the extra details those options need, supplied through an ActionAdvancedInfo implementation and configured in workflow-actions.xml. Examples are assign_eperson (an EPerson lookup on the task page) and rating (a score). edit_metadata predates this framework and does not fit it. Two samples follow: selectrevieweraction, performed by POSTing submit_select_reviewer with one or more eperson ids to the claimed task, and scorereviewaction (maximum score and whether a description is required), performed by POSTing rating with a score and an optional description.

Introduction to the Workflow Definitions endpoints. A workflow definition is set globally or per collection and gives the list of workflow steps for each collection and the default steps. The endpoints need authentication but no specific permission.
/api/config/workflowdefinitions lists the configured workflow definitions.

/api/config/workflowdefinitions/<definition-name> returns one workflow definition, with its name (for example default), whether it is the default, and its type. It links to collections, the collections that explicitly use it, and steps, the workflow steps it includes.
Heading for the search methods of the workflow definitions endpoint.

Search method findByCollection, /api/config/workflowdefinitions/search/findByCollection?uuid=<collection-uuid>, returns the workflow definition that applies to a collection, falling back to the default configuration.
Heading for the linked entities of a workflow definition.

/api/config/workflowdefinitions/<definition-name>/collections lists the collections that explicitly use the workflow definition. A collection that names none gets the default mapping but is not listed.
/api/config/workflowdefinitions/<definition-name>/steps lists the workflow steps used in the definition, as described on the workflow steps page.
Title of the WorkflowItem Endpoints page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.
/api/workflow/workflowitems lists the workflow items. The example is still to be provided.

/api/workflow/workflowitems/<id> returns one workflow item. As with a workspace item, the in-progress submission's data sit in a sections map that follows the submission definition and is open for extension (each section type has its own JSON structure, for example collection, form pages, license, cclicense and uploads with their access conditions); a step attribute gives the workflow step reached. It links to step, collection (where the item will be created), item (which holds the submission data) and submissionDefinition.
Heading for the linked entities of a workflow item.

/api/workflow/workflowitems/<id>/collection is read-only and returns the collection the in-progress submission belongs to. The collection cannot be changed directly once the submission exists; a section such as the enhanced select-collection section planned for DSpace 7 could change it through the sections data. The example is still to be provided.

/api/workflow/workflowitems/<id>/item is read-only and returns the backend item held by the submission. The item cannot be replaced once the submission exists; changes to it show up in the submission automatically but are not checked by submission validation, as they are administrative edits. The example is still to be provided.

/api/workflow/workflowitems/<id>/submissionDefinition is read-only and returns the submission definition used by the in-progress submission, which by default is derived from its collection and follows any change of collection. The same definition can be had from /api/config/submissiondefinitions/search/findByCollection, but this link saves a separate call and leaves room to change the one-to-one link between collections and definitions later without breaking clients. The example is still to be provided.
/api/workflow/workflowitems/<id>/step is read-only and returns the workflow step of the workflow item, as described on the workflow steps page.
Heading for the search methods of the workflow items endpoint.
Search method findBySubmitter, /api/workflow/workflowitems/search/findBySubmitter?uuid=<submitter-uuid>, returns the workflow items created by that submitter.

Search method item, /api/workflow/workflowitems/search/item?uuid=<item-uuid>, returns the workflow item for an item; uuid is mandatory, and since an item has at most one workflow item, the result is a single object, not a list. Responses: 200 OK with the workflow item; 401 if not authenticated; 403 without permission to view it; 204 if there is none.

Starting a workflow: POST the WorkspaceItem's URI, as text/uri-list, to /api/workflow/workflowitems, as in the curl example. Responses: 201 with the new workflow item in the body, or an empty body when no workflow is enabled and the item is available at once; 401 if not authenticated; 403 if the user is not the workspace item's submitter; 422 if the workspace item has validation errors and is not ready for workflow.

A multipart POST to a workflow item usually adds a new file to the section named by the upload variable (uploads by default), handled by that section's implementation. On success it returns 201 with the workflow item's new state.

DELETE /api/workflow/workflowitems/<id> resets the workflow and sends the item back to the workspace, whatever step it had reached; with ?expunge=true the workflow item is deleted instead. Responses: 204 No content; 401 if not authenticated; 403 for non-administrators; 404 if the workflow does not exist.
Introduction to the Workflow Steps endpoints. A workflow step is one step in the review process, such as the accept/reject step. The endpoints need authentication but no specific permission.
/api/config/workflowsteps, the main workflow steps endpoint, is not implemented and returns 405.
/api/config/workflowsteps/<step-name> returns one workflow step, for example editstep, with the list of workflow actions it uses, embedded and linked; see the workflow actions endpoints.

The access section of a WorkspaceItem holds the item's access conditions. The section has the same name as its configuration under /api/config/submissionaccessoptions (a section named itemAccessConditions matches /api/config/submissionaccessoptions/itemAccessConditions). Its data are discoverable (when false, the item is hidden from search, browse and OAI and can be reached only by direct link) and accessConditions (every policy the user applied to the item, each with a name and, where required, start and end dates).
Patch operations on a workspace item take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902); each successful one returns 200 with the new workspace item. The general patch rules apply.

Adding an access condition: a PATCH add on /sections/<form-name>/accessConditions/- appends one, and an add on /sections/<form-name>/accessConditions with an array replaces them all. The attributes required depend on the condition's name, as configured in submissionaccessoptions: for example openaccess needs nothing more, while embargo is rejected without a startDate. Adding at a specific index makes no sense, and the array is never null (at worst empty), so clients can always append.
Removing an access condition: a PATCH remove on /sections/<form-name>/accessConditions/<index> removes one, and a remove on /sections/<form-name>/accessConditions resets them to an empty array.
The replace operation replaces existing information; using it where there is no previous value is an error, per the general patch rules.

Replacing the discoverable flag: a PATCH replace on /sections/<form-name>/discoverable with true or false, for example changing true to false. If the access configuration does not let the user set the item's visibility, the server answers 422.

Replacing an access condition: a PATCH replace can swap a condition for a new one (for example /accessConditions/0 with an embargo and its startDate), change one setting (such as /accessConditions/0/startDate), or change its name (for example openaccess to administrator). The new settings must be valid for the condition's name in submissionaccessoptions; the backend removes the old policy and creates a new one, and a name change works only when both conditions need the same settings, otherwise it fails with 422.

How item and bitstream access conditions relate: access conditions set on a bitstream through the upload section override the item's. A bitstream with no access conditions of its own inherits the item's; one that has its own ignores the item's.

The cclicense section of a WorkspaceItem holds the Creative Commons licence: uri (the licence URI, usually stored in dc.rights.uri), rights (the licence name, usually stored in dc.rights) and file (the bitstream holding the licence). Each is null when no licence has been granted.
Patch operations on the cclicense section take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902); each successful one returns 200 with the new workspace item.

Accepting a Creative Commons licence: a PATCH add of the licence URI, obtained from the Search CC License endpoint, at /sections/<form-name>/uri. dc.rights, dc.rights.uri and the RDF bitstream are then fetched from the Creative Commons API. A later add on the same path replaces the licence: the new one is added to the item and the old one deleted. Using add to replace follows RFC 6902 section 4.1, under which adding to an existing member replaces its value.
Removing a granted Creative Commons licence: a PATCH remove on /sections/<form-name>/uri.

The identifiers section of a WorkspaceItem lists the identifiers assigned to it, in the same structure as the item identifiers link. Each identifier has value (the identifier string, such as a DOI URL), identifierType (such as doi or handle), identifierStatus (where relevant, since some types are minted locally and then reserved or registered upstream) and type (the resource type, for context in the UI). The supported types are doi and handle.
The identifiers section has no PATCH operations; it only reports the identifiers currently assigned to the workspace item.

The license section of a WorkspaceItem holds the deposit licence grant: granted (true or false), url (read-only; where the granted licence can be seen) and acceptanceDate (read-only; the acceptance time recorded in the licence bitstream's dcterms:dateAccepted, null for licences granted before DSpace 7).
Patch operations on the license section take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902); each successful one returns 200 with the new workspace item.

Accepting the deposit licence: a PATCH add of true at /sections/<form-name>/granted, with before and after example documents showing granted, url and acceptanceDate being set. A later add on granted replaces the licence: a new licence bitstream is added and the old one deleted, so url and acceptanceDate change. Adding false rejects or removes the licence. Using add to replace follows RFC 6902 section 4.1.
The licence can also be accepted or rejected by a replace on the granted path with true or false; the curl examples given use the add operation.
Removing a granted licence: a PATCH remove on /sections/license/granted, with example documents before and after.
There is no plan to implement the move, test and copy operations on the license section for now.

The submission-form section of a WorkspaceItem holds the metadata collected by one submission form. Each key is a metadata field in dot form (such as dc.title or dc.contributor.author), and its value is an array ordered by place, each entry with value, authority (the authority key, if any), confidence (the authority confidence, or -1) and language (an ISO code, if any). Archived items model metadata the same way, but in a different place in the JSON, and are changed as described on the Modifying Metadata via PATCH page.
Patch operations on the submission-form section take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902).

Adding metadata in a submission form. A PATCH add on /sections/<form-name>/<metadata>/- appends a value (value, language, authority, confidence) to an existing field, and an add on /<metadata>/<index> inserts it at a zero-based position; worked examples append and then insert authors. A field not yet present must be initialised by adding an array of values at /sections/<form-name>/<metadata>, since appending to a missing path is not allowed; the same call with several values initialises or replaces all of a field's values. Using add to replace follows RFC 6902 section 4.1, and sending an array to the - position would create a nested array element (Appendix A.16).

Removing metadata in a submission form: a PATCH remove on /sections/<form-name>/<metadata>/<index> removes one value, and a remove on /sections/<form-name>/<metadata> removes all values of the field; examples are given.

Replacing metadata in a submission form. Replace changes existing information only; replacing a field not yet set is an error. Examples replace a title value and language at /sections/traditionalpageone/dc.title/0, and change just its language at /dc.title/0/language.
Reordering metadata values: a PATCH move from one index to another, for example moving the third author (/dc.contributor.author/2) to the first position (/dc.contributor.author/0).
There is no plan to implement the test and copy operations on the submission-form section for now.

The sherpaPolicies section of a WorkspaceItem holds the publisher open access policies retrieved from Sherpa/RoMEO: a retrievalTime and a sherpaResponse with the journal metadata (titles, ISSNs, publishers, DOAJ status) and its publisher policies, such as permitted versions, embargoes, licences, conditions and archiving locations. sherpaResponse is never empty; with no results it carries at least an error flag and a message. The section is left out entirely when the item has nothing, such as an ISSN, to query Sherpa/RoMEO with.

Patch operations on the sherpaPolicies section take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902), but the section is almost read-only, since its data come straight from Sherpa; the only accepted change is removing retrievalTime.
Sherpa data are cached to limit load on the Sherpa web services. A PATCH remove of /sections/sherpaPolicies/retrievalTime forces a fresh call.

The upload section of a WorkspaceItem lists the user's uploaded files. Each file has metadata (in the same structure as the submission-form section), sizeBytes and checkSum (algorithm and value; both read-only, computed by the server on receipt), url (read-only; where the file can be downloaded) and accessConditions (the policies the user applied to the file).
Patch operations on the upload section take a JSON Patch body (RFC 6902); each successful one returns 200 with the new workspace item. The general patch rules apply.
In the upload section, add is used to add metadata or access conditions to files already uploaded. A new file is uploaded with a multipart POST to the workspace items endpoint.

Adding file metadata in the upload section works as for the submission form, with the path /sections/<form-name>/files/<file-index>/metadata/<metadata>: append with /-, insert at a zero-based index, or add an array at the field path to initialise or replace all its values. The example sets the first uploaded file's dc.title to MyFile.pdf. More examples are on the submission-form section page.

Adding a file access condition: a PATCH add on /sections/<form-name>/files/<file-index>/accessConditions/- appends one, and an add of an array on the file's access conditions path replaces them all. The attributes needed depend on the condition's name, as configured in submissionuploads: openaccess needs nothing more, while embargo is rejected without a startDate. The array is never null, so clients can always append rather than add at an index.
Removing an uploaded file: a PATCH remove on /sections/uploads/files/<file-index>.
Removing file metadata, or a single value, works as on the submission-form section, using the path to the file's metadata (/files/<file-index>/metadata/).

Removing a file access condition: a PATCH remove on /sections/uploads/files/<file-index>/accessConditions/<index> removes one, and a remove on the file's accessConditions path resets them to an empty array.
In the upload section, replace changes existing information only; replacing something with no previous value is an error, per the general patch rules.
Replacing file metadata, or a single value, works as on the submission-form section, using the path to the file's metadata (/files/<file-index>/metadata/).

Replacing a file access condition swaps it for a new one whose settings must be valid for its name in the submissionuploads configuration; the example sets an embargo with a start date at index 0. The backend removes the old policy and creates a new one; the text says this works only when the old and new conditions need the same settings (as openaccess and administrator do), and otherwise the request fails with 422.
Uploaded files can be reordered with a move on the files index path, for example moving the third file (/files/2) to the first position (/files/0).
Moving a value of a repeatable file metadata field works as on the submission-form section, using the path to the file's metadata (/files/<file-index>/metadata/).
There is no plan to implement the test and copy operations on the upload section for now.
Title of the WorkspaceItem Endpoints page, with a link back to the list of all endpoints.
/api/submission/workspaceitems lists the workspace items. The example is still to be provided.

A multipart POST to /api/submission/workspaceitems creates a workspace item in one of two ways. From a remote resource: a text/uri-list body naming an external entry value (for example an ORCID record), whose metadata is imported straight away with no preview, since the user has already chosen the record and the item starts empty. From files: one or more uploaded files, where files with no parser are discarded, the first parseable file pre-fills the metadata and the others are just attached, and a file holding more than one entry gives 422. curl examples are given for both.

/api/submission/workspaceitems/<id> returns one workspace item. The in-progress submission's data sit in a sections map that follows the submission definition and is open for extension (each section type has its own JSON structure; the example shows collection, identifiers, form pages, license, cclicense and uploads). It links to collection (where the item will be created), item (which holds the data), submissionDefinition and supervisionOrders.

A multipart POST to a single workspace item usually adds a new file to the section named by the upload variable (uploads by default), handled by that section's implementation, and returns 201 with the workspace item's new state. An owning collection may be given; if omitted, the first collection the user can submit to is used.
Heading for the linked entities of a workspace item.

/api/submission/workspaceitems/<id>/collection is read-only and returns the collection the in-progress submission belongs to. The collection cannot be changed directly once the submission exists; a section such as the enhanced select-collection section planned for DSpace 7 could change it through the sections data. The example is still to be provided.

/api/submission/workspaceitems/<id>/item is read-only and returns the backend item held by the submission. The item cannot be replaced once the submission exists; changes to it show up in the submission automatically but are not checked by submission validation, as they are administrative edits. The example is still to be provided.

/api/submission/workspaceitems/<id>/submissionDefinition is read-only and returns the submission definition used by the in-progress submission, which by default is derived from its collection and follows any change of collection. The same definition can be had from /api/config/submissiondefinitions/search/findByCollection, but this link saves a separate call and leaves room to change the one-to-one link between collections and definitions later without breaking clients. The example is still to be provided.
Heading for the search methods of the workspace items endpoint.
Search method findBySubmitter, /api/submission/workspaceitems/search/findBySubmitter?uuid=<submitter-uuid>, returns the workspace items created by that eperson.

Search method item, /api/submission/workspaceitems/search/item?uuid=<item-uuid>, returns the workspace item for an item; uuid is mandatory, and since an item has at most one workspace item, the result is a single object, not a list. Responses: 200 OK with the workspace item; 401 if not authenticated; 403 without permission to view it; 204 if there is none.

DELETE /api/submission/workspaceitems/<uuid> deletes the workspace item and its associated item. Responses: 204 No content; 401 if not authenticated; 403 unless the requester is the submitter or an administrator; 404 if it does not exist.
